catalog_quote: With a few exceptions, stress falls on the penultimate syllable. Examples (50) - (53) illustrate stress placement in non-suspect words. (50) a. /kalova/ [a'lova] tree ... (51) a. /manave-na/ [mana'wena] long ... (52) b. /a-kabi-i-di/ [axa'bidi] I took them ... Phonetically there are many words that appear not to follow the above stress pattern; instead of the stress falling on the penultimate syllable it falls on the antepenult. [...] Phonetically there are many words that appear not to follow the above stress pattern; instead of the stress falling on the penultimate syllable it falls on the antepenult. new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog penultimate stress (penultimate) and adds the domain (stress assigned after suffixation, before final [-a] epenthesis, so many surface forms look antepenultimate), the two lexical exceptions, and the stress-retracted -na noun form.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word as it stands after suffixation but before the word-final epenthetic vowel [-a] is added to consonant-final stems; surface antepenultimate stress in words like ['yabana] 'sky' and [a'bagala] 'I erred' is therefore penultimate at the stage where stress is assigned. Stress moves rightward with each suffix ([a'xabi] ~ [axa'bidi]; [axalu'vila] ~ [axaluvi'lamna] ~ [axaluvilem'nei]).
new_statements.exceptions: Two lexical exceptions (p. 269): /a-bobuala/ [a'bobwara] 'I talk' and /a-uiauana/ [au'yawana] 'I rejoice' have antepenultimate stress in the intransitive form although the stem is not consonant-final (no epenthesis), 'These are the only exceptions that have been found.' Separately, section 4.4 (pp. 313-314): inalienably possessed nouns in the neutralised form with invariant -na take 'a shift in stress one syllable to the left' ([ma'ta-gu] vs ['matana] 'eye', [da'ba-gu] vs ['dabana] 'head', ['nimana] 'hand'), i.e. antepenultimate/initial stress in that construction. Section 2.1.5 (p. 258): /a/ is [ə] in unstressed syllables.
new_statements.identity_note: Olson describes Gumawana as spoken in the Amphlett Islands, Milne Bay Province (the SIL OPD calls it 'Gumawana (Gumasi)', ISO gvs); no dialect split is discussed. The listed SIL OPD (Olson 1992, Ukarumpa) is by the same author as the opened Pacific Linguistics sketch and almost certainly restates the same penultimate rule, but that was not verified because the OPD could not be opened.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding passage, the exception passage and all three secondary locators are present verbatim in the Olson 1992 text we hold at the stated pages (268-269, 258, 313-314). (2) Deciding source: a 1992 Pacific Linguistics reference grammar sketch by the resident SIL fieldworker, the only published grammar of Gumawana per Glottolog; its stress section states penultimate stress with a derivational-ordering account of surface antepenults (C-final stems + epenthetic -a; -na neutralised inalienables) and an explicit closed exception list, which matches our rule string, the primary-stress rule, edge=right and the exceptions statement=listed-set. (3) Better sources: none found.
